extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, USPTO attorneys, and parties involved in USPTO disciplinary proceedings
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and criteria used by the USPTO (OED and Administrative Law Judge) to evaluate alleged professional misconduct by practitioners and to determine sanctions in disciplinary proceedings under 35 U.S.C. § 32 and 37 C.F.R. part 11.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO authority and procedural preconditions for discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: USPTO has the exclusive authority to establish qualifications for admitting persons to practice before it, and to suspend or exclude them from practicing before it; before disciplining a practitioner under 35 U.S.C. § 32, USPTO must provide notice and an opportunity for a hearing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disciplinary hearings are conducted in accordance with 37 C.F.R. part 11 and with section 7 of the Administrative Procedure Act, 5 U.S.C. § 556, by an impartial hearing officer appointed by USPTO. See 37 C.F.R. §§ 11.39, 11.44.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden and standard of proof
rubrics_metrics.description: The OED Director has the burden of proving alleged violations by clear and convincing evidence; the respondent bears the burden of proving any affirmative defenses by clear and convincing evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clear and convincing evidence is an intermediate standard requiring evidence of such weight that it 'produces in the mind of the trier of fact a firm belief or conviction, without hesitancy,' or proves the facts at issue to be 'highly probable.' (Citations: Jimenez v. DaimlerChrysler; Colorado v. New Mexico.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Competence (37 C.F.R. § 11.101)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner must 'provide competent representation,' which requires the legal, scientific, and technical knowledge, skill, thoroughness and preparation reasonably necessary for the representation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to know or apply substantive patent rules (e.g., monitoring PAIR, understanding drawing/photo rules, filing requirements) can demonstrate lack of competence. Past warning letters about monitoring PAIR are relevant to assessing competence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diligence (37 C.F.R. § 11.103)
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner must 'act with reasonable diligence and promptness in representing a client.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific manifestations include timely responding to Office actions, timely paying/filing for extensions where required, forwarding Office notices to client, and generally avoiding neglect that causes abandonment of applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Client communication duties (37 C.F.R. § 11.104(a)(3), (a)(4), (b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner must keep the client reasonably informed, respond to reasonable requests for information, and explain matters to the extent reasonably necessary to allow the client to make informed decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adequate communication includes forwarding notices (e.g., filing receipts, notices of publication, notices of abandonment), explaining Office actions and deadlines, and answering client questions in a way the client can understand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honesty and avoidance of deceit (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner must not engage in conduct involving dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: leading a client to believe a filing or response will occur later when it has already occurred; concealing abandonment; providing inaccurate information about application status. Intentional misrepresentations are higher culpability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct prejudicial to the administration of justice (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner must avoid conduct that is prejudicial to the administration of justice or that reflects negatively on the legal system or the profession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dishonest conduct and concealment reduce public confidence in the profession and the Bar's ability to self-regulate; such harms weigh in discipline determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to monitor docketing/PAIR for client matters
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner should periodically review Private PAIR (or other docketing systems) to note any action upon applications the practitioner assumes responsibility to prosecute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to monitor PAIR and thereby miss mailings or changes in status (publication, office actions, abandonment) is relevant to findings of negligence or lack of competence/diligence; prior warnings about this practice are aggravating evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness and procedural compliance in responding to Office actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Responses to Office actions must be filed within the statutory period or must include a timely request for extension of time and payment of associated government fees; failure to do so can cause abandonment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners must track shortened statutory periods set by examiners and ensure extension requests/fees are timely filed when required. Misstating deadlines to clients or filing untimely responses without required fees is misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper use of drawings and photographs under patent rules (37 C.F.R. § 1.84(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Photographs are not ordinarily permitted in utility patent applications unless they are the 'only practicable medium for illustrating the claimed invention.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Petitions to accept photographs must justify that photographs are the only practical medium and often require accompanying amendments to the specification; failing to meet these requirements can result in petition denial and rejection of the application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirements for petitions (e.g., Petition to Accept Photographs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Petitions under the patent rules (such as to accept photographs) must meet regulatory content requirements (e.g., show photographs are the only practicable medium and include any necessary amendments).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A deficient petition (e.g., lacking required amendment or adequate justification) will be dismissed; filing such a petition untimely or without proper content reflects on practitioner competence and diligence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidentiary nuance: constructive knowledge vs. actual knowledge for intent findings
rubrics_metrics.description: Constructive knowledge (what a competent practitioner should have known) is not alone a basis to infer intent to deceive; actual knowledge or other evidence is required to find intentional dishonesty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Negligence can be found from constructive knowledge; intentional misconduct requires evidence that the practitioner knowingly or deliberately acted to deceive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degrees of culpability (negligent, knowing, intentional)
rubrics_metrics.description: When assessing misconduct, consider whether the practitioner acted negligently, knowingly, or intentionally; intentional misconduct is the highest level of culpability and supports harsher sanctions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allocate findings accordingly: e.g., negligence for missed deadlines; knowing failures to respond to client requests; intentional dishonesty when a practitioner deliberately misleads a client about filings or status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanctioning framework (37 C.F.R. § 11.54(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: In determining an appropriate sanction, the Court must consider: (1) whether the practitioner violated a duty owed to a client, the public, the legal system, or the profession; (2) whether the practitioner acted intentionally, knowingly, or negligently; (3) the amount of actual or potential injury caused by the misconduct; and (4) the existence of any aggravating or mitigating factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court often looks to the ABA Standards for Imposing Lawyer Sanctions for guidance when determining length and severity of sanction or whether aggravating/mitigating factors exist. Compare to precedent cases with similar facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggravating and mitigating factors (ABA Standards §§ 9.22, 9.32 guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aggravating factors can include refusal to acknowledge wrongful conduct and substantial experience; mitigating factors include absence of prior discipline, absence of dishonest/selfish motive, cooperation in investigation, good character, delay in proceedings, and imposition of other penalties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh aggravating vs. mitigating factors to calibrate sanction severity; examples from precedent inform whether suspension length should be increased or decreased.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precedent and proportionality in sanctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts compare the practitioner's misconduct and circumstances to prior disciplinary cases to ensure proportionality of sanctions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For example, similar mishandling causing abandonment and deceit have resulted in six-month suspensions; but corrective actions taken by the practitioner and cooperation may warrant lesser sanctions (e.g., 90-day suspension with probation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Restitution considerations in disciplinary remedies
rubrics_metrics.description: Restitution may be ordered only where the value of the client's loss resulting from the respondent's misconduct is established or where restitution is necessary to prevent unjust enrichment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The central purpose of disciplinary proceedings is to protect the public, not to compensate injured clients; absent demonstrable financial loss or unjust enrichment, restitution is generally declined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duties during suspension and path to reinstatement (37 C.F.R. §§ 11.58, 11.60(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: If suspended, practitioners have specific duties while suspended and must obtain a petition for reinstatement pursuant to the regulations to return to practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The order cites 37 C.F.R. § 11.58 (duties while suspended) and directs that a practitioner remains suspended until the OED Director grants a petition reinstating respondent under § 11.60(c).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence evaluation and sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Findings rely on stipulated facts, documentary evidence (joint and government exhibits), and witness testimony; the decision weighs these against the clear-and-convincing standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include consideration of contemporaneous communications (emails), filing receipts, Office actions, and prior warning letters when assessing whether rules were violated and the practitioner's state of mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to disclose mistakes and the impact of concealment
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners have a duty to be forthright about mistakes; attempts to conceal errors (e.g., hiding abandonment, misrepresenting filing status) constitute dishonest conduct and are aggravating.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concealment aimed at avoiding client anger may explain motive but does not excuse misconduct; intentional concealment supports findings of dishonesty and increases sanction severity.
